title: Red to Green
teaches: Red to green as we trade it: an entry trigger that rides on a setup that already qualifies, a leader pulling back to support above a rising 20-day EMA; the line is the prior day's close, the buy is a market order as price trades a cent over it after trading below it, no more than 4% above, the stop sits a few cents under the dip's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, and a loss at the stop is the plan working.

questions.q: Which price is the red-to-green line?
choices: The prior day's close
Today's opening price
Today's running VWAP
The prior day's high
questions.why: The prior day's official close. Red to green is a move from below the previous close to above it, at least one cent over during regular hours. The line is never the day's open or VWAP. The prior day's high is a different level.
questions.lesson_line: The line is yesterday's close.

wrong.Today's opening price: A green candle is close over open. The red-to-green line is the prior close, never the open.
wrong.Today's running VWAP: Our card says the line is the prior close, never VWAP.
wrong.The prior day's high: The high is a different level. The line is the prior close.

choices: An entry trigger on a setup

A gap-up continuation setup

questions.answer: An entry trigger on a setup
questions.why: An entry trigger on a setup. Our card calls red to green one of four entry triggers. It rides on a setup that already qualifies. That setup is a leader above the 200-day with a rising 20-day EMA, pulling back into support. The cross of the prior close is only the trigger. With no setup under it, it is not a trade.

wrong.A standalone base pattern: A base is a setup. Red to green is the entry for a stock that already qualifies.
wrong.A gap-up continuation setup: Red to green starts from a gap down or a red open, not a gap up.

Buy and widen the stop

questions.q: Is light volume a no-trade?
choices: No, volume is a cue, not a gate
Yes, 0.6x is too thin to trust
Yes, wait until volume rises
No, light volume is ideal
questions.answer: No, volume is a cue, not a gate
questions.why: No. Our card has no hard volume rule. Higher volume on the reclaim and a wider range are a plus, graded. Light volume lowers the grade but does not cancel the trade. In our data, ANF crossed on 0.6x volume and still reached 3R in 2 days.
questions.lesson_line: Volume grades the cross. It does not gate it.

wrong.Yes, 0.6x is too thin to trust: There is no hard volume rule. In our data, ANF crossed on 0.6x volume and still reached 3R in 2 days.
wrong.Yes, wait until volume rises: Our card has no hard volume rule. The trigger is the cross; volume only grades it.
wrong.No, light volume is ideal: Higher volume on the reclaim is the plus. Light volume is a small minus, not a gate.

questions.story: A leader flagged on its 20-day EMA, gapped down and crossed the prior close in the first hour. Volume is 0.6x of average.
questions.simple: No, because volume only raises or lowers the grade, and light volume alone does not cancel the trade.

deeper.example: ANF, 2026-10-08, from our own bars. It opened at 137.72 against a prior close of 139.44 and crossed on 0.6x volume. The buy was 139.45 with the stop at 137.69, 1.3% away. Light volume was its one blemish, and it reached 3R in 2 days. One case does not prove light volume is fine. It shows volume grades the trade rather than gating it.

reasons: the volume line is a card proposal and the example is one the owner has not reviewed (+2)

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Size down by the stop, or skip it
Usual size; the setup is clean
Pull the stop up to 3% and buy
Skip; a stop must be under 1%
questions.answer: Size down by the stop, or skip it
questions.why: Size down by the stop, or skip. Our card keeps the stop within about 3% of the entry, and this honest stop is 3.44% under the buy. The size comes from the stop, so a wider stop means fewer shares. Never pull the stop above the dip's low to make it fit.
questions.lesson_line: Size from the honest stop.

wrong.Usual size; the setup is clean: A clean setup does not shrink the honest stop. The size comes from the stop, so a 3.44% stop means fewer shares.
wrong.Pull the stop up to 3% and buy: A stop pulled above the dip's low is not the honest stop. If the honest stop does not fit, skip or size down.
wrong.Skip; a stop must be under 1%: Our line is about 3%, not 1%. The 1% is the median stop, not a rule.

questions.story: A leader gaps down onto its 20-day EMA and crosses. The honest stop under the dip's low is 3.44% under the buy.
questions.simple: Size down or skip, because the honest stop is 3.44% away, past our line of about 3%.

deeper.example: DELL, a near-miss: a 3.4% gap down to the 20-day EMA, with the stop at 397.66, 3.44% under the buy at 411.81. The dip was too deep for the stop. Our card calls it the edge of the gap setups: skip or size down by the stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A13) and our card

questions.q: A green close. Was the stop wrong?
choices: No, a green close is not a free pass
Yes, you should have sold at the close
Yes, the stop should have been wider
No, but use a mental stop next time
questions.answer: No, a green close is not a free pass
questions.why: No. A green close is not a free pass. The stop at 179.43 was still about 1.2% under the 181.60 buy, and one red open took it. The stop is the exit and only moves up. A green close does not make the stop wrong, and no rule says sell at the close.
questions.lesson_line: A green close does not move the stop.

wrong.Yes, you should have sold at the close: No rule sells at a green close. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up.
wrong.Yes, the stop should have been wider: Never a stop wider than the dip's low. The stop only moves up.
wrong.No, but use a mental stop next time: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.

questions.story: You bought at 181.60 with the stop at 179.43. The day closed green. The next morning it opened red and traded down through the stop.
questions.simple: No. The stop did its job, because a green close does not protect a trade from the next day's drop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, D41)

questions.q: What grade?
choices: B-minus; the 20-day EMA is falling
A+; the cross came in hour one
No trade; the gap is too small
questions.why: B-minus at best. A flat or falling 20-day EMA is a B-minus cue. The setup is a pullback in a trend, not a bounce in a correction.
questions.lesson_line: Rising 20-day, or the grade drops.

wrong.A+; the cross came in hour one: A quick cross helps, but a falling 20-day EMA is a B-minus cue.
wrong.No trade; the gap is too small: The card does not rest on a gap size here. The falling 20-day EMA is what costs the grade.

questions.story: A stock above its 200-day gaps down 1% and crosses in the first hour. But its 20-day EMA is falling and it sits 13% under its 50-day.

questions.q: What helped this red to green?
choices: The market gapped, then got bought
The stock was a weak metals laggard
The cross came late, after lunch
Volume dried up as it crossed the line
questions.answer: The market gapped, then got bought
questions.why: The market gapped down and got bought the same morning. Our card lists that as a cue in favor of a red to green. In the CDE case, a metals leader flagged four days on its 9-day EMA and crossed in hour one. The market had gapped down and was bought the same morning.
questions.lesson_line: A dip the whole market buys is stronger.

wrong.The stock was a weak metals laggard: A laggard hurts, not helps. We buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more.
wrong.The cross came late, after lunch: A slow, late cross grades lower. A quick cross is the plus.
wrong.Volume dried up as it crossed the line: Higher volume on the reclaim is the plus, not lower. Our card has no hard volume rule.

questions.simple: The market gapping down and getting bought the same morning helped, because our card counts that as a plus.

reasons: rests on a proposed card cue
fixed before: 2026-11-10 cold check

questions.q: Red to green or Oops?
choices: An Oops reversal first
A plain red to green
Red to green: over the open
A Go Signal on the reclaim
questions.why: An Oops reversal first. An Oops opens below the prior day's low and reclaims that low. A red to green only needs a dip under the prior close and a trade back over it. This stock has reclaimed the low, not the prior close. If it later trades over the prior close, that is a red to green too.
questions.lesson_line: Under the low and back is an Oops.

wrong.A plain red to green: It reclaimed the prior low, not the prior close. An undercut of the prior low that is reclaimed is an Oops first.
wrong.Red to green: over the open: Over the open is not over the line. The line is the prior close, never the open.
wrong.A Go Signal on the reclaim: A Go Signal is a red to green with a timer and a level. This has not crossed the prior close yet.

questions.story: The stock opened under yesterday's low and reclaimed that low by 10:15. It is still under yesterday's close.
questions.simple: It is an Oops first, because it opened under yesterday's low and won that low back.

deeper.trap: The trap is calling any reclaim a red to green. Reclaiming yesterday's low is an Oops. The red-to-green line is yesterday's close, which sits higher. One day can be both: an Oops at the low, then a red to green if price later trades over the close.

reasons: rests on our card's look-alike line

questions.q: Red to green or Go Signal?
choices: A red to green, not a Go Signal
A Go Signal off the 2 pm cross
An Oops reversal at the open bar
Neither; a cross after noon is void
questions.answer: A red to green, not a Go Signal
questions.why: A red-to-green trigger. A cross at 2 pm, or with no flag under it, is a trigger, not a Go Signal. A Go Signal is the red to green with a timer and a level. A late cross is not void either: we have no time-of-day rule. It only grades lower.
questions.lesson_line: No flag, no timer: only a trigger.

wrong.A Go Signal off the 2 pm cross: A Go Signal is the red to green with a timer and a level. A 2 pm cross with no flag under it is a trigger.
wrong.An Oops reversal at the open bar: An Oops opens under the prior day's low. This one opened above it.
wrong.Neither; a cross after noon is void: We have no time-of-day rule. A late cross is still a trigger. It only grades lower.

questions.story: It opened 1% under the prior close, above yesterday's low. The cross came at 14:00. There was no tight hourly flag under it.
questions.simple: It is a plain red to green, because a 2 pm cross with no flag lacks a Go Signal's timer and level.

reasons: rests on our card's look-alike line and the owner's rulebook (C30)
fixed before: variety rewrite 2026-11-10

questions.q: Can a Kicker be a red-to-green entry?
choices: No, it never starts under the line
Yes, it is the cleanest of all
Yes, if it gaps up on huge volume
No, its line is today's open
questions.answer: No, it never starts under the line
questions.why: No. A Kicker opens above the prior close and never trades back to it, so it cannot go red to green. Red to green needs a start under the prior close. The line is always the prior close, never the day's open.
questions.lesson_line: Red to green needs a red start.

wrong.Yes, it is the cleanest of all: A Kicker is never red at the open, so it cannot cross the line from below.
wrong.Yes, if it gaps up on huge volume: Volume changes nothing. A Kicker still opens above the prior close and never starts under the line.
wrong.No, its line is today's open: The line is always the prior close, never the open. A Kicker never trades back to the prior close.

questions.story: A Kicker gaps up and trades through the prior day's high at the open. Someone calls it the cleanest red to green.
questions.simple: No, because a Kicker opens above yesterday's close and never dips under it, so it never starts red.

reasons: the Kicker's place in the course is a held owner decision (D-010)
fixed before: variety rewrite 2026-11-10

questions.q: Buy it on the green tick?
choices: Pass; it is a big news gap down
Buy; it passed the prior close
Buy; leaders bounce after gaps
Pass; wait for a green close
questions.answer: Pass; it is a big news gap down
questions.why: Pass. Buying a big news gap down because it ticked green is a named mistake on our card. The cross is only a trigger, riding on a setup that already qualifies. A fraud probe and a guidance cut are news, not a pullback into support. QuantRocket's test points the same way: stocks tend to keep dropping after large down gaps.
questions.lesson_line: A big news gap down is not a red-to-green buy.

wrong.Buy; it passed the prior close: The cross is only a trigger, and it needs a setup under it. A news gap down is not a pullback.
wrong.Buy; leaders bounce after gaps: QuantRocket's test found the reverse: stocks tend to keep dropping after large down gaps.
wrong.Pass; wait for a green close: A green close is not our trigger. The reason to pass is the news gap, a named mistake on our card.

questions.story: A leader gaps down hard on a fraud probe and a guidance cut. At 10:40 it ticks back over the prior close.
questions.simple: Pass, because buying a big news gap down just because it ticked green is a named mistake on our card.

deeper.trap: The trap is the green tick. A stock down hard on news can trade back over the prior close. The cross is a trigger, and it needs a setup under it. A gap on a fraud probe is news, not a pullback, so the trigger has nothing to ride on.

reasons: tied to a held decision on the gap ceiling, D-133 (+2)
fixed before: the gap number was removed (+1)

questions.q: Short it?
choices: No, no shorts above the 200-day
Yes, it is the mirror of red to green
Yes, if you keep the stop tight
No, not until it closes under the line
questions.why: No. Never short a green to red in a leader above the 200-day. In the Go Signal that move is the shakeout before the long. Our rulebook allows shorts only below the 200-day, unless it is a parabolic short.
questions.lesson_line: Green to red in a leader is a shakeout.

wrong.Yes, it is the mirror of red to green: No shorts above the 200-day, mirror or not. In a leader, that drop is the shakeout before the long.
wrong.Yes, if you keep the stop tight: A tight stop does not change the rule. No shorts above the 200-day.
wrong.No, not until it closes under the line: A close changes nothing. Shorts are only below the 200-day, and this leader is above it.

questions.story: A leader above its 200-day opens green and falls through the prior close in the first hour.
questions.simple: No, because we never short a leader above its 200-day, and in the Go Signal that drop is a shakeout.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating a green to red as the mirror of a red to green and shorting it. In a leader above the 200-day, that drop through the prior close is the shakeout before the long. Our rulebook allows shorts only below the 200-day, unless it is a parabolic short.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: Take the cross?
choices: Pass; nothing is under the dip
Take it; the cross was in hour one
Take it with a wider stop
Wait; buy on the close if it holds
questions.answer: Pass; nothing is under the dip
questions.why: Pass. The dip should tag support, its low within 1% of a level. Here the dip low, 188.24, sat 2.9% above the nearest level, the prior day's low at 182.94. That is a trigger with no setup under it. A quick cross helps the grade, but it cannot replace the level.
questions.lesson_line: A cross with no level under it is only a trigger.

wrong.Take it; the cross was in hour one: A quick cross helps the grade. It cannot replace a level under the dip.
wrong.Take it with a wider stop: The stop is never set wider to give room. And there is still no setup under the dip.
wrong.Wait; buy on the close if it holds: A close does not put a level under the dip. With no support under it, there is no setup to buy.

questions.story: A leader gaps down 1.4% and crosses in the first hour. The dip low is 188.24. The nearest level, the prior day's low, is 182.94.
questions.simple: Pass, because the dip stopped far above any support level, so the cross has no setup under it.

deeper.trap: The trap is a fast first-hour cross that looks strong, so the support check gets skipped. In the PLTR near-miss the dip low sat 2.9% above the nearest level, and the rule is within 1%. A cross like that is a trigger with no setup under it.

reasons: rests on our card
the key compares against a proposed 1% tag distance (the dossier's number)

questions.q: Take the cross?
choices: Pass; a report is 3 sessions away
Take it; the setup is clean
Take it, sell before the report
Pass; no buys in a report month
questions.answer: Pass; a report is 3 sessions away
questions.why: Pass. Our rulebook says no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report, and this report is 3 sessions away. A clean setup does not lift that, and a plan to sell before the report does not either. The window is only the days before a report. A post-earnings flag is after the report, which is fine.
questions.lesson_line: Clean cross, near report: no buy.

wrong.Take it; the setup is clean: A clean setup does not lift the earnings window.
wrong.Take it, sell before the report: A plan to sell later does not lift the rule. No new buys in the 3 days before a report.
wrong.Pass; no buys in a report month: The rule covers only the 3 days before a report. A buy after a report, in a post-earnings flag, is fine.

questions.story: A leader gaps down onto its 50-day and crosses in the first hour. Its report is due 3 sessions from now.
questions.simple: Pass, because we make no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report.

deeper.trap: The trap is a clean setup that tempts you to buy now and sell before the report. The rule is no new buys in the 3 days before a report. You may hold through a report only if the trade is already up 5R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Which cross grades higher?
choices: The 9:50 cross that held the line
The 13:30 cross after chopping
Same grade; there is no time rule
Neither one is a valid red to green
questions.answer: The 9:50 cross that held the line
questions.why: The 9:50 cross that held the line. Our card has no time-of-day rule, but timing is a grading factor. A quick cross inside the first hour that does not chop back and forth is the stronger case. A slow, grinding cross long after the open is the weaker one. A higher grade is not a promise: in our data the first-hour cross is the fast one and the whippy one.
questions.lesson_line: Quick and clean beats slow and choppy.

wrong.The 13:30 cross after chopping: A slow, grinding cross long after the open is the weaker cross.
wrong.Same grade; there is no time rule: There is no time-of-day rule, but a quick cross is still a grading factor. The clean first-hour cross grades higher.
wrong.Neither one is a valid red to green: Both are valid crosses. Timing grades the trade; it does not void it.

questions.story: Cross A came at 9:50, off a 0.9% gap down, and held above the line. Cross B came at 13:30 after the stock chopped across the line four times.
questions.simple: The 9:50 cross, because a quick, clean cross in the first hour grades higher than a slow cross after chopping.

deeper.trap: A higher grade does not promise a better result. Our own data calls the first-hour cross the fast one and the whippy one. The grade says which cross fits the picture we want. The stop still handles the rest, whichever cross you take.

reasons: grade cues are discretionary under the owner's E50 (+2)
fixed before (+1)

questions.q: Which red to green grades higher?
choices: A, the stronger case
B, it has more room to run
They grade the same
B, the index gap hurts A
questions.why: A. Setup A is a true leader, RS 94, above a rising 20-day, 50-day and 200-day. The index gapped down and got bought, and the cross was quick. Setup B has RS 74, under our floor of 80, so it is not a leader at all.
questions.lesson_line: Leader, rising average, level and market all line up.

wrong.B, it has more room to run: B is not a leader. RS 74 is under 80.
wrong.They grade the same: A is a leader and B is not.
wrong.B, the index gap hurts A: An index that gaps down and gets bought the same morning is a cue in favor. And B is not a leader: RS 74 is under 80.

questions.story: Setup A: RS 94, above a rising 20-day, 50-day and 200-day, the index gapped down and got bought, a quick cross. Setup B: RS 74, a flat 20-day, not at a level, a late cross.
questions.simple: A grades higher, because B has an RS of 74, under 80, so it is not a leader.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)
fixed before: 2026-11-10 cold check

questions.q: The stop fills at 12:30. Was the trade a mistake?
choices: No, a planned loss at the stop
Yes, the stop was too tight
Yes, the red close proves it
No, but skip first-hour crosses
questions.answer: No, a planned loss at the stop
questions.why: No. You bought the first-hour cross at 194.80 with the stop at 190.33. The stop came first and the size came from it, so this loss was planned. The first-hour cross is the fast one and the whippy one. The stop is the exit, and it did its job.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out under the rules is a planned loss.

wrong.Yes, the stop was too tight: A 2.29% stop is inside our about 3%. Widening a stop to give it room is a mistake our card names.
wrong.Yes, the red close proves it: The stop filled at 12:30, before the close. The loss was the one you sized for when you set the stop.
wrong.No, but skip first-hour crosses: We have no time-of-day rule. A quick cross in the first hour is a plus in the grade, even if it is the whippy one.

questions.story: The setup met every rule. You bought the first-hour cross at 194.80 with the stop at 190.33. The second hour closes back under the line and the stop fills at 12:30. The day closes red.
questions.simple: No, because you followed the rules and the stop capped the loss where you planned.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging a rule by one result. AMD on 2024-03-14 crossed in hour one and the 12:30 bar took its 2.29% stop. The first-hour cross is the fast one and the whippy one. The stop came first and the size came from it, so the loss was planned.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4) and our card

questions.q: Should you have sold when it fell back under the line?
choices: No; the stop was the planned exit
Yes; back under the line means sell
Yes; sell on an hourly close under it
No; but lower the stop next time
questions.answer: No; the stop was the planned exit
questions.why: No. Our card treats even a close back under the prior close as a warning sign, not an exit. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up. Here the stop did the selling at 15:30.
questions.lesson_line: Under the line is a warning. The stop is the exit.

wrong.Yes; back under the line means sell: Back under the line is a warning, not an exit. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Yes; sell on an hourly close under it: Even a close back under the prior close is a warning, not an exit. The stop is the exit.
wrong.No; but lower the stop next time: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.

questions.story: You bought the cross at 424.08 with the stop at 416.07. It slipped back under the line and stayed there. The stop filled at 15:30.
questions.simple: No, because slipping under the line is a warning, and the stop you set was the exit.

deeper.counter: Slipping back under the line is a warning sign, not the exit. On TSLA, 2025-01-22, it spent the whole day under the line and the stop went in the last hour. The stop did the selling, at the price you planned.

reasons: rests on our card and the owner's failed-reclaim ruling (D-136, settled as a warning)

questions.q: Take the retry?
choices: Yes, a new trade with its own stop
No, the first stop-out ends the name
Yes, bigger, to make the loss back
No, wait a month after a stop-out
questions.answer: Yes, a new trade with its own stop
questions.why: Yes. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. The cap is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock. You have had none this week. In the TWLO case, the retry on 2026-09-15 at the same level ran 14.8R.
questions.lesson_line: A retry is a new trade, inside the cap.

wrong.No, the first stop-out ends the name: The cap is 3 tries a week and 6 a month. One stop-out two weeks ago does not end it.
wrong.Yes, bigger, to make the loss back: A retry is a new trade with every rule. The size comes from its own stop, never from the last loss.
wrong.No, wait a month after a stop-out: A retry needs only a new trigger, as a new trade with every rule. The cap is 3 tries a week and 6 a month.

questions.story: A leader was stopped out the same day at its 20-day EMA two weeks ago. Today it gaps down onto the same level and crosses again. You have had no tries this week.
questions.simple: Yes, because a fresh trigger is a new trade with its own stop, and you are under the weekly try limit.

deeper.example: TWLO on 2026-09-02 met every rule at the 20-day EMA, crossed in hour one and was stopped the same day, best 0.6R. The retry on 2026-09-15, at the same level, ran 14.8R. One case proves nothing, but it shows why a stop-out does not end a name.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21, E56)

questions.q: Take the cross?
choices: Pass; the 20-day EMA is falling
Take it; it crossed the line
Take it with a smaller stop
Pass; it needs a bigger volume day
questions.why: Pass. Our card wants a rising 20-day EMA: today's value above the value 5 sessions ago. Here it is under its value 5 sessions ago, and the stock is rolling over. That is a bounce in a correction, not a pullback in a trend. The cross is only a trigger, so with no setup under it there is no trade.
questions.lesson_line: Rising 20-day, or no pullback in a trend.

wrong.Take it; it crossed the line: The cross needs a setup under it. A falling 20-day is a bounce in a correction.
wrong.Take it with a smaller stop: A tighter stop does not fix a missing setup. The 20-day EMA must be rising.
wrong.Pass; it needs a bigger volume day: There is no hard volume rule. It fails because the 20-day EMA is falling, a bounce in a correction.

questions.story: A stock gaps down and crosses the prior close in the first hour. Its 20-day EMA is under its value 5 sessions ago, and the stock is rolling over.
questions.simple: Pass, because a falling 20-day average means a bounce in a correction, not a pullback in an uptrend.

deeper.trap: The trap is a cross that looks like every other cross. In the APP near-miss the 20-day EMA, 612.33, sat under its value 5 sessions earlier, 624.73. Under a falling 20-day, a cross is a bounce in a correction, not a pullback in a trend.

reasons: rests on a proposed card gate; the card also lists a falling 20-day EMA as a grade row (q42 was cut over it)

questions.q: Take it?
choices: Yes, take it: setup and trigger pass
Pass; it opened red under the line
Buy at the open, before the cross
Wait for it to clear yesterday's high
questions.answer: Yes, take it: setup and trigger pass
questions.why: Yes. A leader above its 200-day pulls back four sessions to a rising 20-day EMA, and the dip to 83.60 tags it. It dips under the 85.00 prior close and trades back over it. The market is Green and no report is near. The stop goes a few cents under the 83.60 dip low.
questions.lesson_line: Setup and trigger both in: take the trade.

wrong.Pass; it opened red under the line: Opening red is how a red to green starts. It needs a dip under the line before the cross.
wrong.Buy at the open, before the cross: Buying under the line in anticipation is a named mistake. Wait for the trade over the prior close.
wrong.Wait for it to clear yesterday's high: The red-to-green line is the prior close, 85.00, and price is already over it.

questions.story: A leader above its 200-day pulls back four sessions to its rising 20-day EMA. It opens at 84.10 against a prior close of 85.00, and the dip to 83.60 tags the EMA. It trades over 85.00 in the first hour and closes the day over it. The market is Green and the report is weeks away.
questions.simple: Take it, because the setup and the trigger are both there.

deeper.trap: The trap is passing because it opened red. Opening under the line is how a red to green starts. The setup is in place and price is back over 85.00, so the trigger is in. The stop a few cents under the 83.60 dip low is the exit.

reasons: tied to a held decision on the trigger, D-003 (+2)
rests on the owner's rulebook, E57 and F65 (+2)
fixed before (+1)

questions.q: The day before a gap down. The daily chart shows the pullback and averages, not RS or the hourly cross. Watch or pass?
choices: Watch; the 20-day EMA is rising
Pass; the 20-day EMA is falling
Pass; it is under the 200-day
Watch; buy the open if it gaps
questions.why: Watch for the cross. The 20-day EMA is rising under a two-week drift down to it, and price sits above the 200-day. That is the setup on a daily chart. The chart cannot show RS or the hourly cross, so the leader test and the trigger still come next. The next day it gapped down onto its 20-day EMA, with a wide green first hour.
questions.lesson_line: A pullback to a rising 20-day is the setup.

wrong.Pass; the 20-day EMA is falling: Look again: the 20-day EMA is rising under the pullback.
wrong.Pass; it is under the 200-day: Price sits above the 200-day, resting on its 20-day EMA.
wrong.Watch; buy the open if it gaps: The buy is the cross of the prior close, not the open. Buying under the line in anticipation is a named mistake.

questions.simple: Watch for the cross, because the stock has drifted down to a rising 20-day EMA, which is the setup.

deeper.trap: A rising 20-day EMA is the setup, not the buy. The daily chart cannot show RS or the hourly cross. So you still check the leader test and the report date, and the buy waits for a trade over the prior close.

reasons: the rising 20-day gate is a card proposal and the example is one the owner has not reviewed (+2)
fixed before (+1)

questions.q: The day before a gap down. The daily chart shows the 20-day EMA, not RS or the hourly cross. Watch or pass?
choices: Pass; the 20-day EMA is falling
Watch for the cross; it is a leader
Watch; it is above the 200-day
Pass; too far over the 200-day

The line you bought over

questions.story: Your risk math says 40,000 shares, and the 40% position cap allows more. The stock trades 3,000,000 shares a day on average.
choices: 30,000, the volume ceiling
40,000, the risk math
20,000 now, 10,000 more later
40,000; the ceiling is a guide

wrong.40,000, the risk math: That is over 1% of 3,000,000 shares. The size is the smaller number, so the ceiling caps it.
wrong.20,000 now, 10,000 more later: No adding. The full size goes in at one price with one stop.
wrong.40,000; the ceiling is a guide: Our market reading is a guide. The volume rule is not: we never own more than 1% of daily volume.

questions.simple: 30,000 shares, because we never own more than 1% of the daily volume, and 1% of 3,000,000 is 30,000.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating the risk math as the final number. It only says how many shares fit your risk. Then the ceilings apply: here 1% of the daily volume. Whichever number is smaller is the size.

reasons: a computed key (+2)

questions.q: Where does the stop on the rest go?
questions.story: You bought the red to green at 96.36 with the stop at 94.67. The stock runs and you make your first sell, part of the position.
choices: Up to your fill price, breakeven
Stay put under the dip's low
Up to the price you sold at
Just under the 9 EMA
questions.answer: Up to your fill price, breakeven
questions.why: Up to your fill price, 96.36, which is breakeven. Our rule moves the stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first sell by default. You have just made the first sell, so the stop goes to the fill now. It does not jump to the price you sold at, and the 9 EMA trail is only for what is left.
questions.lesson_line: At the first sell, the stop moves up to breakeven.

wrong.Stay put under the dip's low: At the first sell the stop moves up to breakeven by default.
wrong.Up to the price you sold at: That locks in a profit target as a stop. Breakeven is the fill price.
wrong.Just under the 9 EMA: The 9 EMA is the trail for what is left, not the breakeven move.

questions.simple: Up to your fill price of 96.36, because the stop moves to breakeven at the first sell.

questions.lesson_line: Breakeven waits for 2R at least, not the first profit.
questions.simple: False. Breakeven waits until the trade is up at least 2R, usually at the first trim.

questions.lesson_line: Write your 5R price down. It is a mark to measure from.
questions.simple: 117.83, because one R is 111.93 minus 110.75, and adding five of those to the fill lands there.

reasons: a computed key (+2)
rests on the owner's rulebook, E51 (+2)

Sell a third more, by the rule
Sell all the rest and bank the 5R
Add a third more at the new high

questions.lesson_line: At 5R, a later sell is a judgment. Trail what is left.

wrong.Sell all the rest and bank the 5R: What is left is trailed, not all sold at a mark.
wrong.Add a third more at the new high: The full size is bought at one price. No adding.

questions.q: Complete the trail rule.

questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 9 EMA. Steadier name, 20 EMA.
questions.simple: What is left of a fast mover is sold on a close under its 9 EMA.

questions.q: Do you sell what is left?
questions.story: You hold what is left of a red-to-green winner. It is a steady name that has ridden its 20 EMA for weeks. Today it closes under the 9 EMA but above the 20 EMA.
choices: No, hold; the 20 EMA is its trail
Yes, a close under the 9 EMA exits
Yes, sell half of what is left
No, hold; trail the 50-day instead
questions.answer: No, hold; the 20 EMA is its trail
questions.why: No. Our default trail is the 9 EMA for fast movers and the 20 EMA for steadier ones. This name has ridden its 20 EMA for weeks, so the 20 EMA is its trail. Sell what is left on a close below that line, not below the 9 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Pick the trail that fits the stock. Sell on a close under it.

wrong.No, hold; trail the 50-day instead: The defaults are the 9 EMA and the 20 EMA, not the 50-day.
wrong.Yes, a close under the 9 EMA exits: The 9 EMA trails fast movers. This steady name trails the 20 EMA.
wrong.Yes, sell half of what is left: The rule is a sale on a close under the trail average, not a half step.

questions.simple: No, hold, because a steady name trails its 20 EMA, and it is still above that line.

deeper.trap: The close under the 9 EMA looks like an exit, and for a fast mover it would be. But this name has ridden its 20 EMA for weeks. Pick the line that fits how the stock moves, then sell only on a close below that line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, E52 (+2)

questions.lesson_line: The trail sells on a close, not a touch.
questions.simple: True. It takes a close under the average to sell what is left, not a dip under it during the day.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought a red to green ten trading days ago and it closed green that day. Since then it has drifted and sits at 0.5R. The stop has not traded.
choices: Sell; under 1R after 10 days
Hold; the green close proved it
Hold; the stop has not traded yet
Add to it; it is still up 0.5R
questions.why: Sell. Our time stop sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days, freeing the money. This one sits at 0.5R. The green close on day one does not change that. The time stop works even when the price stop has not traded. No adding: full size goes in at one price.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days under 1R and the trade is done. The money moves on.

wrong.Hold; the green close proved it: The green close was on day one. After 10 trading days under 1R, the time stop sells it.
wrong.Hold; the stop has not traded yet: The time stop is its own exit. Under 1R after 10 days, it is sold before the stop trades.
wrong.Add to it; it is still up 0.5R: No adding: full size at one price. The time stop sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days.

questions.simple: Sell, because after 10 trading days it is still under 1R, so the time stop frees the money.

deeper.trap: The trap is holding because nothing has gone wrong. The price stop has not traded and day one closed green, so it feels fine. But a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.lesson_line: No position over 40% of the account.
